segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was the word for "what"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Qué.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Qué.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "What", when it's not a question, is lo que. Lo que.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, if you want to say, "I saw what you're doing." This is not a question,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: no? "I saw what you're doing." Here, the "what" is not a question. Here it's lo que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I cooked what they're eating." "I cooked what they're eating."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Here "what" is not a question, no? Yo cociné, "I cooked", lo que comen, or lo que están comiendo if we mean right now.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "what", not as a question, is lo que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say, "I don't want you to speak about what we spoke about"? But, you know, we don't need this "about".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, the first bit is "I don't want you to speak." And let's speak informally: "I don't want you to speak. I don't want that you speak."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que hables.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No quiero que hables. "about"

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it de?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: De, you could use, or you could use...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sobre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sobre. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, no quiero que hables de, or sobre, "what we spoke about." And we can just say "what we spoke".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo que hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes, it's the same in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So give it to me now altogether: "I don't want you to speak about what we spoke about." From the beginning and thinking it through again.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablamos, or no quiero que hables de lo que hablamos. Good. But that sentence could be ambiguous, no? I mean, in your mind, when you're creating this sentence, you will have the context very strongly in your mind that you're thinking about what we spoke about the other day. But that doesn't necessarily mean that the person receiving it has that same context in their mind. They might, depends what your conversation is about. But if you don't have a context that's shared, it could be ambiguous. You could understand, "I don't want you to speak about what we speak about," generally, because of course we have hablamos, which can be past or present. No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablamos, generally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So there's two ways here that you could clarify. You could add something like "the other day", el otro día. No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablamos el otro día. So, you are showing with some time expression that it was past. Or you could use the line in the past: "what we were speaking about", because here it's interchangeable. The meaning changes so slightly, and both meanings are fine, no? If we look at the English: "I don't want you to speak about what we were speaking about." "I don't want you to speak about what we spoke about." So maybe here in Spanish you choose the line in the past just so it's obvious that you're talking about the past. So let's give it another go using the line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I don't want you to speak about what we were speaking about." "I don't want you to speak" - informally still.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No quiero que hables sobre lo que hablábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "necessity", "necessity" in Spanish is - do you remember what to do with -ity words to make them Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: -idad.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So "necessity" becomes...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesidad.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Necesidad.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To need" is necesitar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesitar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I need"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesito.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Necesito. "I need you to prepare it." Let's speak formally. "I need you to prepare it", formally.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: In English again it would be "I need that you prepare it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesito que lo prepare.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Necesito que lo prepare. This is to you, formally. If you wanted to make it clear that you were speaking to you and not speaking about him or her,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: how would you do that here? "I need you to prepare it."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesito que usted lo prepare.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. Necesito que usted lo prepare. Necesito que lo prepare usted. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So with quiero que, necesito que, we're seeing two things that they have in common. We have a verb like quiero, necesito, a verb that's showing what we want to occur in the world, expressing our subjectivity, let's say, in this way. And we have the structural similarity that the mood tense is coming after que.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To be short of", "to be short of", "to be missing", "to lack", is faltar. Quite uncomfortable translations, but this is a very common verb in Spanish: faltar. It's used very often, this verb, in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For example, you could say: "I need you to prepare what's missing. I need you to prepare what's missing, what's leftover, what we need to do still", huh?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So again formally: "I need you to prepare..."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Necesito que prepare...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "...what's missing."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...lo que falta.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Necesito que prepare lo que falta. And lo que because the "what" here is not a question. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The noun is also used quite often. The noun is falta, la falta. So falta means "lack", "lack".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So if I say falta de consideración, what does it mean? Falta de consideración.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Oh right, "lack of consideration".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "lack of consideration". It's also used with "respect", falta de respeto, "lack of respect".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And it's also used in the expression hace falta: "it makes lack", "it makes lack", which just is another way of saying "it's necessary", but it's very common.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And hace falta que, of course, is followed by this mood tense. In the same way that we do with quiero que, necesito que, we will follow it with this mood tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, if you wanted to say, using hace falta, "It is necessary that we eat soon" - what was the word for "soon"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it pronto? Or is that Italian?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That's That's it. In Italian actually it means "ready", pronto. This is why when Italians answer the phone, they say "pronto" because historically, let's say, there was a operator there connecting the wires and they were there going "Ready? Are you ready? Is it ready? Can you hear me?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But in Spanish it's "soon", like the British slang people say in England, "Get here pronto, get here soon."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "it makes lack", hace falta, huh? "It makes lack that we eat soon."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Sorry, can you explain again, how why does that make sense? "It makes lack that we eat soon"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "It makes lack" would be the literal translation, but literal translations are often uncomfortable, no? Especially when we're talking about fixed expressions. So hace falta is an extremely common expression, quite difficult to translate comfortably, just another way of saying "it's necessary".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So "it makes lack", or hace falta, "that we eat soon" - how would it be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hace falta que comamos pronto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hace falta que comamos pronto. So hace falta you will hear around a lot, and falta as a noun, you will hear it in especially in phrases like falta de respeto, "a lack of respect", you hear that a lot.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And faltar as a verb, "to lack" or "to be missing", is also very useful.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To prefer" in Spanish is preferir. Preferir.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Preferir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Preferir. How is "I prefer"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It should be...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefiero.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Better. Prefiero. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So again, if you say "I prefer him to stay", we're not going to say "I prefer him to stay", we will say "I prefer that he stays", and what what are we going to do with "he stays"? I think you're getting the gist now.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Mood tense.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mood tense. So it's not just the structures that we are identifying, it's the feeling. This is very important for the mood tense. What you want to really get your head around is the feeling of the mood tense, so you can start experimenting about where you would use it, and listening out for where you hear people using it.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I prefer that he stays. I prefer for him to stay, I prefer that he stays."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefiero que se queda... sorry, quede.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Prefiero que se quede.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I prefer them to stay. I prefer for them to stay."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefiero que se queden.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Prefiero que se queden. "I prefer that they don't stay here", huh? "I prefer that they don't stay here, I prefer for them not to stay here."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefiero que se... que no se queden aquí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Prefiero que no se queden aquí. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say "I prefer you to give it to him. I prefer you", speaking informally, "to give it to him."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: So it's "I prefer that you give it to him."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefiero que lo le... ah... se lo des.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That's it!

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Prefiero que se lo des.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So this could mean "I prefer you to give it to him, to her..." How would we clarify it if we want to show it's "to him"? "I prefer you to give it to him."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Prefiero que se lo des a él.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. And what if it was "to her"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A ella. Prefiero que se lo des a ella.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Prefiero que se lo des a ella. Very good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to clarify, we can then say a él, a ella to show afterwards who we meant with se.
